items.title: Article 368 — The Amendment Procedure
items.body:
### Amending the Constitution

**In one line**
An amendment is a formal, written change to the Constitution, and **Article 368** is the rule-book that says who can make such a change and how.

**Why it is asked**
The exam loves to test the small procedural details — where a bill starts, what majority is needed, and whether the President can say no. One or two prelims questions almost every year come from here.

**The story**
The makers of the Constitution did not want it to be frozen forever, nor changed on a whim. So they placed the power to amend in **Parliament** (not with the states, not with the people through a referendum) and wrote the steps in **Article 368**, which sits in **Part XX**. The idea of this graded procedure was borrowed from the **South African Constitution**.

Step by step: an amendment bill may be introduced in **either House** of Parliament (Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha) — never in a State Legislature — and needs **no prior permission of the President**. Each House must pass it on its own by the required majority; there is **no joint sitting** if the two Houses disagree. Earlier the President could sit on the bill, but the **24th Amendment (1971)** made assent **compulsory** — today the President must sign and cannot withhold or return it.

How big a majority is needed depends on what is being changed. There are three routes, from easiest to hardest.

**Picture it**

| Route | Majority needed | What it changes |
|---|---|---|
| Simple majority (outside Article 368) | More than half of the members present and voting | New states, citizenship, quorum, salaries |
| Special majority | More than half of the **total** membership of a House **and** two-thirds of those **present and voting** | Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles |
| Special majority + state approval | The above **plus** approval by at least half the State Legislatures | Federal matters — President's election, Seventh Schedule, Centre-state powers |

Only the last two are counted as amendments **under Article 368**. Simple-majority changes are technically ordinary laws, not constitutional amendments.

**Terms explained**
- **Ratification** — formal approval. Here it means at least half of the State Assemblies must separately pass the bill before a federal change takes effect.
- **Special majority** — two conditions at once: over 50% of the whole House, and two-thirds of only those voting that day.
- **Quorum** — the minimum number of members who must be present for the House to do business.

**Don't confuse**
- Introduced only in **Parliament**, never in a State Legislature (a common trap).
- State approval is needed from **half** the states, **not all** of them.
- The President's assent is **mandatory** (since 1971), unlike an ordinary bill which the President may return once.

**Remember it**
Three majorities, in order of difficulty: **Simple → Special → Special-plus-States** (S-S-S).

**TL;DR**
- Article 368 (Part XX) governs amendments; the procedure idea came from South Africa.
- A bill starts only in Parliament, in either House; no joint sitting.
- 24th Amendment (1971) made the President's assent compulsory.
- Three routes: simple majority, special majority, special majority plus approval by half the states.
keyPoints: Article 368 (Part XX) governs amendments; procedure idea borrowed from South Africa.
An amendment bill can be introduced only in Parliament, in either House, not in State Legislatures.
24th Amendment (1971) made the President's assent to an amendment bill mandatory.
Special majority = over 50% of total membership of a House + two-thirds of members present and voting.
Federal provisions additionally need approval by at least half the State Legislatures.
Simple-majority changes (new states, citizenship) fall outside the scope of Article 368.

items.title: Landmark Constitutional Amendments
items.body:
### The amendments the exam keeps asking

**In one line**
A handful of amendments changed the Constitution so deeply that their numbers and years are standard exam facts.

**Why it is asked**
Match-the-following and 'which amendment did X' questions are almost guaranteed. Knowing the number, the year and the one-line change is enough to score.

**The story**
Since 1951 the Constitution has been amended **106** times (as of 2026). Most were routine, but a few reshaped the document. The very **first** amendment (1951) created the **Ninth Schedule** to shield land-reform laws from court challenge. The **42nd (1976)**, passed during the Emergency, made so many changes that it is nicknamed the **'Mini-Constitution'**. The **44th (1978)** undid several Emergency-era excesses. Later amendments brought in local government (73rd and 74th), the GST (101st), and reservations (103rd, 105th, 106th). The **106th (2023)**, the Women's Reservation Act, is the **latest** amendment as of 2026.

**Picture it**

| Amendment | Year | Key change |
|---|---|---|
| 1st | 1951 | Added Ninth Schedule; Articles 31A and 31B (land reform) |
| 7th | 1956 | Reorganisation of states — 14 states, 6 Union Territories |
| 42nd ('Mini-Constitution') | 1976 | Socialist, Secular, Integrity in Preamble; Fundamental Duties (Part IVA); All-India Judicial Service |
| 44th | 1978 | Right to property made a legal right (Article 300A); shields Articles 20 and 21 in emergency |
| 52nd | 1985 | Anti-defection law, Tenth Schedule |
| 61st | 1989 | Voting age lowered from 21 to 18 |
| 73rd | 1992 | Constitutional status to Panchayati Raj institutions; added the **Eleventh Schedule** |
| 74th | 1992 | Urban local bodies (municipalities); added the **Twelfth Schedule** |
| 86th | 2002 | Right to Education (Article 21A) |
| 91st | 2003 | Capped Council of Ministers at 15%; tightened anti-defection |
| 101st | 2016 | Goods and Services Tax (GST) |
| 102nd | 2018 | Constitutional status to the National Commission for Backward Classes |
| 103rd | 2019 | 10% reservation for economically weaker sections |
| 105th | 2021 | Restored states' power to identify backward classes |
| 106th | 2023 | Women's Reservation (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam) — one-third of seats in the **Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies** |

**Terms explained**
- **Ninth Schedule** — a list of laws placed beyond ordinary court challenge; created by the 1st Amendment.
- **Fundamental Duties** — a list of citizens' moral duties, added as Part IVA by the 42nd Amendment.
- **Economically weaker sections (EWS)** — people below an income/asset limit who are not covered by caste-based reservation.

**Don't confuse**
- 'Socialist' and 'Secular' were added by the **42nd (1976)**, not the 44th.
- The **61st** lowered the voting age; the **86th** brought Right to Education — easy to swap.
- 73rd = Panchayats = **Eleventh** Schedule; 74th = municipalities = **Twelfth** Schedule — both passed in the same year, 1992.
- 103rd = EWS, 105th = backward-class identification, 106th = women. Keep the trio straight.

**Remember it**
Reservation trio: **103rd = EWS, 105th = backward classes, 106th = Women**.

**TL;DR**
- 1st (1951) added the Ninth Schedule; 42nd (1976) is the 'Mini-Constitution'.
- 44th (1978) made the right to property a legal right under Article 300A.
- 101st (2016) brought GST; 103rd (2019) brought 10% EWS reservation.
- 106th (2023) reserves one-third of seats for women — the latest amendment as of 2026 (106 in total).
keyPoints: 1st Amendment (1951) added the Ninth Schedule and Articles 31A/31B.
42nd Amendment (1976), the 'Mini-Constitution', added Socialist/Secular/Integrity and Fundamental Duties.
44th Amendment (1978) made the right to property a legal right under Article 300A.
61st Amendment (1989) lowered the voting age from 21 to 18.
73rd and 74th Amendments (1992) gave constitutional status to Panchayats and urban local bodies.
101st (2016) introduced GST; 103rd (2019) gave 10% EWS reservation.
106th Amendment (2023) reserves one-third of seats for women — the latest amendment as of 2026.

items.title: The Basic Structure Doctrine
items.body:
### The Basic Structure Doctrine

**In one line**
Parliament can change the Constitution, but it cannot change the Constitution's core identity — that protected core is called the 'basic structure'.

**Why it is asked**
It is the single most important idea in Indian constitutional law and a favourite of both prelims (which case? which year?) and mains (discuss and evaluate). 

**The story**
Through the 1960s and 1970s a tug-of-war ran between Parliament, which wanted a free hand to amend, and the Supreme Court, which worried that an unlimited power could be used to destroy democracy itself. The clash was settled in **Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)**. A **13-judge bench** — the largest in Indian history — ruled that Parliament may amend **any** part of the Constitution **but cannot damage or destroy its basic structure**. The judgment date, **24 April 1973**, later became a cut-off date in other cases.

The Court deliberately did **not** give a closed list of what the basic structure contains; judges have filled it in case by case. Features recognised so far include the supremacy of the Constitution, the republican and democratic form of government, the secular character of the state, federalism, separation of powers, **judicial review**, the rule of law, free and fair elections, and the unity and integrity of the nation.

Later cases strengthened the doctrine. **Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975)** was the **first** case to actually strike down a constitutional provision using the test — a clause of the 39th Amendment that put the Prime Minister's election beyond the courts was void for breaking free and fair elections. **Minerva Mills (1980)** struck down clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368 and held that limited amending power and judicial review are themselves basic features — 'the Constitution, not Parliament, is supreme'. **Waman Rao (1981)** said the test applies to amendments made after 24 April 1973, and **I.R. Coelho (2007)** held that laws added to the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 can be **tested against the basic structure** — the Ninth Schedule is not a permanent shield (nor was it struck down).

**Picture it**

| Case | Year | What it did for the doctrine |
|---|---|---|
| Kesavananda Bharati | 1973 | Created the doctrine (13 judges) |
| Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain | 1975 | First used it to strike a provision |
| Minerva Mills | 1980 | Judicial review is part of it |
| Waman Rao | 1981 | Applies to post-24-April-1973 amendments |
| I.R. Coelho | 2007 | Ninth Schedule laws now reviewable |

**Terms explained**
- **Doctrine** — a principle laid down by courts through judgments, not written in the Constitution.
- **Judicial review** — the power of courts to check whether a law or amendment is constitutional.
- **Basic structure** — the Constitution's unchangeable core identity; open-ended and judge-defined.

**Don't confuse**
- The basic structure is **not defined** in the Constitution — it is judge-made.
- Kesavananda **allowed** amendment of Fundamental Rights (it only barred destroying the core); it did not freeze them.
- The **first** case to apply the doctrine was Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975), not Kesavananda itself.

**Remember it**
Kesavananda = '**13 judges, 1973**' — the birth of the basic structure.

**TL;DR**
- Kesavananda Bharati (1973), a 13-judge bench, created the Basic Structure Doctrine.
- Parliament can amend any part but cannot destroy the Constitution's basic structure.
- The core is open-ended: supremacy, federalism, secularism, separation of powers, judicial review, rule of law.
- Indira Gandhi (1975) first applied it; Minerva Mills (1980) and I.R. Coelho (2007) reinforced it.
keyPoints: Kesavananda Bharati (1973), a 13-judge bench, propounded the Basic Structure Doctrine.
Parliament can amend any part but cannot destroy the Constitution's basic structure.
Elements include supremacy of the Constitution, federalism, secularism, separation of powers, judicial review and rule of law.
Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975) first applied the doctrine to strike a constitutional provision — the 39th Amendment clause on the PM's election.
Minerva Mills (1980) struck down Article 368 (4) and (5) and affirmed judicial review as basic.
I.R. Coelho (2007) made post-24-April-1973 Ninth Schedule laws reviewable.
items.mnemonic: Kesavananda = '13 judges, 1973' — the birth of basic structure.

items.title: Amendability of Fundamental Rights — The Case Line
items.body:
### Can Parliament amend Fundamental Rights?

**In one line**
The courts changed their mind three times on whether Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights, and the final position is 'yes, but it cannot touch the basic structure'.

**Why it is asked**
The sequence of cases is a classic match-the-following and statement-based theme; getting the order right (1951 → 1967 → 1973) is the whole battle.

**The story**
The question was simple to state but hard to settle: are Fundamental Rights (Part III) beyond Parliament's amending power, or not? In **Shankari Prasad (1951)** the Supreme Court said Parliament **can** amend them, reasoning that a constitutional amendment is not an ordinary 'law' under Article 13(2). **Sajjan Singh (1965)** agreed. Then in **Golaknath (1967)** the Court reversed itself and said Parliament **cannot** amend Part III to take away Fundamental Rights, treating an amendment as 'law'. Parliament hit back with the **24th Amendment (1971)**, declaring it could amend any part. The matter finally settled in **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)**, which **overruled Golaknath**: an amendment is not ordinary 'law', so Fundamental Rights can be amended — but no amendment may destroy the basic structure. Later, **Minerva Mills (1980)** confirmed judicial review as basic, and **I.R. Coelho (2007)** opened post-1973 Ninth Schedule laws to review.

**Picture it**

| Case | Year | Holding |
|---|---|---|
| Shankari Prasad | 1951 | Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights |
| Sajjan Singh | 1965 | Reaffirmed Shankari Prasad |
| Golaknath | 1967 | Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights |
| Kesavananda Bharati | 1973 | Overruled Golaknath; amendable but not the basic structure |
| Minerva Mills | 1980 | Judicial review is part of the basic structure |
| I.R. Coelho | 2007 | Ninth Schedule laws (post-1973) reviewable |

**Terms explained**
- **Article 13(2)** — bars the state from making 'law' that takes away Fundamental Rights; the whole fight was over whether an amendment counts as such 'law'.
- **Overruled** — a later judgment cancels an earlier one as the governing rule.
- **Part III** — the chapter of the Constitution containing Fundamental Rights.

**Don't confuse**
- Shankari Prasad said 'can'; Golaknath said 'cannot'; Kesavananda said 'can, but not the core'. Order matters.
- The 24th Amendment (1971) came **after** Golaknath and **before** Kesavananda.
- Golaknath did **not** survive — Kesavananda overruled it.

**Remember it**
Amendability tug-of-war: '**Can (1951) → Cannot (1967) → Can, but not the core (1973)**'.

**TL;DR**
- Shankari Prasad (1951) and Sajjan Singh (1965): Fundamental Rights are amendable.
- Golaknath (1967): they are not amendable.
- Kesavananda (1973) overruled Golaknath and added the basic-structure limit.
- The 24th Amendment (1971) was Parliament's response asserting its amending power.
keyPoints: Shankari Prasad (1951) and Sajjan Singh (1965) upheld Parliament's power to amend Fundamental Rights.
Golaknath (1967) held Fundamental Rights unamendable, treating an amendment as 'law' under Article 13.
Kesavananda Bharati (1973) overruled Golaknath and introduced the basic-structure limit.
The 24th Amendment (1971) affirmed Parliament's power to amend any part and made assent mandatory.
Parliament's amending power is wide but bounded by the basic structure.
items.mnemonic: Amendability tug-of-war: 'Can (1951) -> Cannot (1967) -> Can, but not the core (1973)'.

items.title: Article 368 in Full — Which Route Amends Which Provision
items.body:
## The three routes, provision by provision

**In one line:** Article 368 in **Part XX** lets Parliament amend the Constitution by special majority, and for federal provisions it also needs half the states; a third route, simple majority, is used for many Articles but is **not** an amendment "under Article 368".

**Why it is asked:** UPSC 2013 and 2022 asked exactly these steps — where the bill starts, whether the President's prior recommendation is needed, whether the President may refuse, and how many states must ratify.

**The story**

### Steps of an Article 368 amendment
- Introduced in **either House** of Parliament — never in a state legislature.
- Can be moved by a **minister or a private member**; **no prior recommendation of the President** is needed.
- Each House passes it **separately** by special majority; there is **no joint sitting** in case of deadlock.
- Federal provisions then need **ratification by half of the state legislatures**, each by a **simple majority**; the Constitution sets **no time limit** for the states.
- The President **must give assent** — made obligatory by the **24th Amendment (1971)**; the President can neither withhold assent nor return the bill.
- The 24th Amendment also added that Parliament amends in exercise of its **constituent power**.
- The procedure was borrowed from **South Africa** (which also gave India the election of Rajya Sabha members).

### Which route for which provision
| Route | Provisions |
|---|---|
| **Simple majority** (outside Art 368) | Admission or establishment of new states (Art 2); formation and changes of states (Art 3); **creation or abolition of Legislative Councils (Art 169)**; Second Schedule emoluments; **quorum** in Parliament; salaries of MPs; rules of procedure; privileges of Parliament; use of English in Parliament; number of puisne SC judges; more jurisdiction to the SC; **citizenship**; elections and **delimitation**; UTs; **Fifth and Sixth Schedules** |
| **Special majority** | **Fundamental Rights**, **Directive Principles** and every provision not in the other two rows |
| **Special majority + half the states** | **Election of the President** and its manner; extent of executive power of the Union and states; **Supreme Court and High Courts**; distribution of legislative powers; **GST Council**; any list in the **Seventh Schedule**; **representation of states in Parliament**; **Article 368 itself** |
- Special majority = a **majority of the total membership** of each House **and** **two-thirds of members present and voting**.

### Criticisms of the procedure
- No special body such as a constitutional convention — the power lies with **Parliament**.
- The **states cannot initiate** an amendment (except asking for a Legislative Council under Art 169).
- No time frame for ratification, no joint sitting, and the procedure is vague in places.
- Still, the blend makes the Constitution **partly rigid and partly flexible**.

## Don't confuse
- Ratification needs **half** the states, **not all** of them (UPSC 2013).
- Prior recommendation of the President — **not needed** for an amendment bill, though it is needed for a bill under Art 3.

**TL;DR**
- Art 368, Part XX; either House; minister or private member; separate special majority; no joint sitting.
- Half the states by simple majority, no time limit; assent obligatory since the 24th Amendment.
- Simple majority: Art 2, 3, 169, quorum, citizenship, delimitation, Fifth/Sixth Schedules — not "amendments" under Art 368.
keyPoints: An amendment bill can be moved by a minister or a private member in either House, needs no prior recommendation of the President and has no joint sitting.
Federal provisions need ratification by half of the state legislatures, each by simple majority, and the Constitution fixes no time limit for them.

Ratification is needed for the election of the President, the Supreme Court and High Courts, the Seventh Schedule lists, the GST Council, representation of states in Parliament and Article 368 itself.
Creation or abolition of Legislative Councils (Art 169), quorum, citizenship, delimitation and the Fifth and Sixth Schedules are changed by simple majority, outside Article 368.
The 24th Amendment (1971) made the President's assent obligatory and described the amending power as constituent power.
The states cannot initiate an amendment, which is a standard criticism of the procedure.

items.title: Amendments 1st to 44th — Act by Act
items.body:
## The first 44 amendments (1951-1978)

**In one line:** the early amendments protected land reform, reorganised states, absorbed new territories, and in the 1970s swung from the Emergency-era **42nd** to the corrective **44th**.

**Why it is asked:** match-the-amendment questions and the UPSC 2019 trap (39th, not 44th, barred courts from the PM's election) come from this table.

**The story**

| Amendment (Act year) | Change |
|---|---|
| **1st** (1951) | **Ninth Schedule**; Art **31A** and **31B**; Art **15(4)** for backward classes; new restrictions on free speech (public order, friendly relations with foreign states) — PM **Nehru** |
| **2nd** (1952) | Readjusted representation in the Lok Sabha |
| **3rd** (1954) | Concurrent List entry on trade in **essential commodities** |
| **5th** (1955) | President may fix a **time limit** for a state to give its views on an Art 3 bill |
| **6th** (1956) | Taxes on **inter-state sale** of goods added to the Union List |
| **7th** (1956) | Abolished Part A, B, C and D states; **14 states and 6 UTs**; **common High Court** for two or more states; Art **350A** (mother-tongue instruction) and **350B** (Special Officer for linguistic minorities) |
| **9th** (1960) | Ceded **Berubari** to Pakistan (East Pakistan) |
| **10th** (1961) | Incorporated **Dadra and Nagar Haveli** |
| **11th** (1961) | **Vice-President** elected by an **electoral college**, not a joint sitting; a vacancy in the electoral college cannot void a presidential election |
| **12th** (1962) | Incorporated **Goa, Daman and Diu** |
| **13th** (1962) | **Nagaland** — Art **371A** |
| **14th** (1962) | Incorporated **Puducherry**; legislatures for some UTs (Art 239A) |
| **15th** (1963) | High Court judges' retirement age **60 to 62**; retired HC judges as **acting judges (Art 224A)**; HC writs beyond its territory |
| **16th** (1963) | "**Sovereignty and integrity**" as grounds to restrict Art 19 freedoms; added to the oaths |
| **18th** (1966) | "State" in Art 3 includes a **UT** |
| **19th** (1966) | Abolished **Election Tribunals** — election petitions go to High Courts |
| **21st** (1967) | **Sindhi** added to the Eighth Schedule (15th language) |
| **22nd** (1969) | Autonomous state of **Meghalaya** within Assam (Art 244A) |
| **24th** (1971) | Parliament may amend **any part, including Fundamental Rights**; President's **assent obligatory** — answer to **Golaknath** |
| **25th** (1971) | Replaced "**compensation**" by "**amount**"; inserted **Art 31C** |
| **26th** (1971) | Abolished **privy purses** and the recognition of former rulers |
| **27th** (1971) | Special provisions for **Manipur** (Art 371C); UT legislatures for Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh |
| **28th** (1972) | Ended the special privileges of **ICS** officers |
| **30th** (1972) | Civil appeals to the SC on a **substantial question of law**, not on money value |
| **31st** (1973) | Lok Sabha raised from **525 to 545** |
| **32nd** (1973) | **Art 371D and 371E** for **Andhra Pradesh** — equal opportunities in jobs and education, an **Administrative Tribunal**, and a **Central University** (after the **Six-Point Formula**, 1973) |
| **33rd** (1974) | Resignation of MPs and MLAs accepted only if **voluntary and genuine** |
| **35th** (1974) | **Sikkim** an **associate state** (Tenth Schedule of that time) |
| **36th** (1975) | **Sikkim** a full state (Art **371F**) |
| **38th** (1975) | Declaration of **emergency** and **ordinances** made **non-justiciable** |
| **39th** (1975) | Disputes over the election of the **PM and Speaker** put beyond courts (Art **329A**) |
| **40th** (1976) | Parliament may fix limits of **territorial waters and the EEZ** |
| **41st** (1976) | Retirement age of **SPSC** members **60 to 62** |
| **42nd** (1976) | **Mini-Constitution** — see below |
| **43rd** (1977) | Restored the jurisdiction of the SC and HCs cut by the 42nd |
| **44th** (1978) | Undid Emergency excesses — see below |

### The 42nd Amendment (1976), "Mini-Constitution"
- **Socialist, Secular, Integrity** in the Preamble; **Fundamental Duties** (Part IVA, Art 51A).
- New DPSPs: **Art 39A** free legal aid, **Art 43A** workers' participation in management, **Art 48A** environment.
- **Tribunals** (Part XIVA, Art 323A and 323B); tenure of the Lok Sabha and Assemblies raised from **five to six years**.
- President **bound by cabinet advice** (Art 74); five subjects moved to the **Concurrent List**; **Art 368(4) and (5)** barred courts from reviewing amendments; Art 31C widened to all Directive Principles; Lok Sabha seats frozen till the **2001** census.

### The 44th Amendment (1978)
- **Right to property** removed from Part III (Art 19(1)(f) and 31 deleted) — now a legal right in **Art 300A**.
- "**Armed rebellion**" replaced "internal disturbance"; emergency only on the cabinet's **written advice**.
- **Art 20 and 21** cannot be suspended in an emergency; the President may return cabinet advice **once** for reconsideration.
- Lok Sabha term restored to **five** years; **Art 361A** protects media reports of Parliament.

## Don't confuse
- **39th** barred courts from the PM's election, not the 44th (UPSC 2019).
- **24th** (1971) answered Golaknath; **25th** introduced Art 31C; **26th** ended privy purses.

**TL;DR**
- 1st (1951) Ninth Schedule under Nehru; 7th (1956) 14 states and 6 UTs; 24th assent obligatory.
- 32nd (1973) Art 371D/371E for Andhra Pradesh; 36th Sikkim; 42nd Mini-Constitution; 44th Art 300A.
keyPoints: The 1st Amendment (1951) added the Ninth Schedule, Art 31A, 31B and 15(4) under PM Nehru; the 7th (1956) created 14 states and 6 UTs and allowed a common High Court.
The 11th Amendment (1961) provided for election of the Vice-President by an electoral college; the 15th (1963) raised the HC retirement age from 60 to 62.
The 24th Amendment (1971) let Parliament amend Fundamental Rights and made assent obligatory; the 25th replaced "compensation" by "amount"; the 26th abolished privy purses.
The 32nd Amendment (1973) inserted Art 371D and 371E for Andhra Pradesh after the Six-Point Formula.
The 42nd Amendment added Art 39A, 43A and 48A, tribunals (Part XIVA), six-year House terms and Art 368(4) and (5).
The 44th Amendment deleted the right to property from Part III (now Art 300A), substituted armed rebellion and protected Art 20 and 21 in emergencies.

items.title: Amendments 45th to 106th — Act by Act, the Recurring Groups & 2026 Status
items.body:
## From anti-defection to women's reservation (1980-2023)

**In one line:** later amendments built local government (73rd, 74th), reservations (77th-103rd), tax reform (80th, 101st), judicial appointments (99th, struck down) and women's reservation (106th, the latest).

**Why it is asked:** almost every APPSC/UPSC paper has a "which amendment" item from this run.

**The story**

| Amendment (Act year) | Change |
|---|---|
| **52nd** (1985) | **Anti-defection** law — **Tenth Schedule** |
| **54th** (1986) | Raised **salaries of judges** and let Parliament change them by law |
| **58th** (1987) | Authoritative **Hindi text** of the Constitution (Art 394A) |
| **61st** (1988) | **Voting age** cut from **21 to 18** (in force 28 March 1989) |
| **65th** (1990) | Multi-member **National Commission for SCs and STs** (Art 338) |
| **69th** (1991) | **National Capital Territory of Delhi** — Assembly and council of ministers (Art 239AA) |
| **70th** (1992) | Delhi and Puducherry MLAs join the **presidential electoral college** |
| **73rd** (1992) | **Panchayats** — Part IX, **Eleventh Schedule**; in force **24 April 1993** |
| **74th** (1992) | **Municipalities** — Part IXA, **Twelfth Schedule**; in force **1 June 1993** |
| **75th** (1994) | **Rent control tribunals** (Art 323B) |
| **76th** (1994) | Tamil Nadu's **69%** reservation law placed in the Ninth Schedule |
| **77th** (1995) | **Reservation in promotion** for SCs and STs — Art **16(4A)** |
| **80th** (2000) | **Alternative scheme of devolution** — all central taxes shared (10th Finance Commission) |
| **81st** (2000) | Unfilled reserved vacancies carried forward as a **separate class** — Art 16(4B), ignoring the 50% ceiling |
| **82nd** (2000) | **Relaxation of qualifying marks** in promotions for SCs and STs (Art 335) |
| **83rd** (2000) | No SC reservation in **Arunachal Pradesh** panchayats |
| **85th** (2001) | **Consequential seniority** in promotions for SCs and STs |
| **86th** (2002) | **Right to Education** for ages **6-14** (Art **21A**); Art 45 early childhood care; Fundamental Duty **51A(k)** |
| **88th** (2003) | **Service tax** (Art 268A) |
| **89th** (2003) | Separate **National Commission for STs** (Art **338A**) |
| **91st** (2003) | Council of Ministers capped at **15%** of the House (a state minimum of **12**); split exemption deleted; defectors barred from remunerative political posts |
| **93rd** (2005) | Reservation in **educational institutions**, including **private unaided** ones (Art **15(5)**) — minority institutions excluded |
| **94th** (2006) | A **tribal welfare minister** for **Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand** (Bihar dropped) |
| **97th** (2011) | **Cooperative societies** — Art 19(1)(c), Art **43B**, Part **IXB** |
| **98th** (2012) | **Hyderabad-Karnataka** region — Art **371J** |
| **99th** (2014) | **National Judicial Appointments Commission** — struck down in 2015 |
| **100th** (2015) | **Land Boundary Agreement** with **Bangladesh** — enclaves exchanged |
| **101st** (2016) | **GST** — Art 246A, 269A, **279A** |
| **102nd** (2018) | Constitutional status to the **National Commission for Backward Classes** (Art **338B**) |
| **103rd** (2019) | Up to **10%** reservation for **EWS** — Art 15(6), 16(6) |
| **104th** (2019) | SC/ST seat reservation extended to **2030**; **Anglo-Indian** nominations ended |
| **105th** (2021) | Restored the **states' power to identify SEBCs** (Art 342A) |
| **106th** (2023) | **Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam** — **one-third** of seats for women in the Lok Sabha, Assemblies and Delhi Assembly (Art **330A**, **332A**, **334A**), for **15 years** |

### Recurring groups
| Group | Amendments |
|---|---|
| SC/ST seat reservation extended (Art 334) | **8th** (to 1970), **23rd** (1980), **45th** (1990), **62nd** (2000), **79th** (2010), **95th** (2020), **104th** (2030) |
| Eighth Schedule languages | **21st** Sindhi; **71st** Konkani, Manipuri, Nepali; **92nd** Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, Santali (total **22**); **96th** "Oriya" became "**Odia**" |
| Special provisions (Art 371) | 371A Nagaland (13th), 371C Manipur (27th), 371D/E Andhra Pradesh (32nd), 371F Sikkim (36th), **371G Mizoram (53rd)**, **371H Arunachal (55th)**, **371I Goa (56th)**, 371J Karnataka (98th) |
| Seat freeze and delimitation | 42nd froze seats till **2001**; **84th** (2001) extended the freeze to **2026**; **87th** (2003) used the **2001** census for readjusting constituencies |
| Punjab President's Rule extended | 48th, 59th, 64th, 67th, 68th |

### Status in October 2026
- Total amendment Acts: **106**; the **106th** is still the latest. The Centre brought it into force from **16 April 2026**.
- The **Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026**, tied to expanding Lok Sabha seats by delimitation, was **defeated in the Lok Sabha in April 2026** — it failed to get a two-thirds majority.
- The **129th Amendment Bill (2024)** on **One Nation, One Election** and the **130th Amendment Bill (2025)** on removal of a PM, CM or minister held in custody for **30 days** are with **Joint Parliamentary Committees**.

## Don't confuse
- **61st** voting age; **86th** Right to Education; **91st** 15% cap; **97th** cooperatives.
- **102nd** gave NCBC status; **105th** restored the states' power — opposite directions.

**TL;DR**
- 52nd Tenth Schedule; 73rd/74th local bodies; 77th-85th SC/ST promotion; 101st GST; 103rd EWS; 106th women (latest).
- Art 334 chain ends at 2030 (104th); 92nd made 22 languages.
keyPoints: The 52nd Amendment (1985) added the Tenth Schedule; the 61st (1988) cut the voting age from 21 to 18.
The 77th (1995) allowed reservation in promotion (Art 16(4A)); the 81st carried forward unfilled vacancies; the 82nd relaxed qualifying marks; the 85th gave consequential seniority.
The 89th Amendment (2003) created a separate National Commission for STs under Art 338A; the 102nd (2018) gave constitutional status to the NCBC under Art 338B.
The 93rd Amendment (2005) allowed reservation in private unaided educational institutions under Art 15(5); the 97th (2011) dealt with cooperative societies.
The 104th Amendment extended SC/ST seat reservation to 2030 and ended Anglo-Indian nominations; the 84th extended the delimitation freeze to 2026.
As of October 2026 there are 106 amendment Acts; the 106th came into force on 16 April 2026, and the 131st Amendment Bill was defeated in the Lok Sabha in April 2026.

items.title: Basic Structure — The Full Case Line, Benches & Elements
items.body:
## How the courts built the basic structure

**In one line:** after twenty years of back-and-forth, **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** held that Parliament can amend every part of the Constitution but not its basic structure, and later cases kept adding elements to that core.

**Why it is asked:** bench sizes, majorities, which case added which element, and the NJAC and EWS rulings are asked in statement and match formats.

**The story**

### The case line
| Case (year) | Holding |
|---|---|
| **Shankari Prasad** (1951) | Upheld the **1st Amendment**; an amendment is not "law" under Art 13 — Fundamental Rights can be amended |
| **Sajjan Singh** (1965) | Upheld the **17th Amendment**; same view |
| **Golaknath** (1967) | **11 judges**, **6:5**, CJ **K. Subba Rao** — Fundamental Rights cannot be abridged; applied **prospective overruling** |
| **Kesavananda Bharati** (24 April 1973) | **13 judges**, **7:6**, CJ **S.M. Sikri**; petitioner the head of the **Edneer Mutt** in Kerala, against Kerala land reform laws; upheld the **24th Amendment**, overruled Golaknath, created the **basic structure** doctrine; the **Preamble** is part of the Constitution |
| **Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain** (1975) | Struck down **Art 329A(4)** (39th Amendment) — **free and fair elections** are basic |
| **Minerva Mills** (1980) | CJ **Y.V. Chandrachud**; struck **Art 368(4) and (5)** and the wider Art 31C; **limited amending power** and **harmony between Fundamental Rights and DPSPs** are basic |
| **Waman Rao** (1981) | Amendments and Ninth Schedule laws **before 24 April 1973** stay valid; later ones face the test |
| **P. Sambamurthy v. State of AP** (1987) | Struck the clause of **Art 371D** that let the **State Government** modify or annul the **Administrative Tribunal**'s orders — against **judicial review** and the rule of law |
| **Kihoto Hollohan** (1992) | Upheld the Tenth Schedule; struck **para 7** (bar on courts) — the Speaker's decision is open to judicial review |
| **Indra Sawhney** (1992) | **Rule of law** is basic; 50% ceiling on reservation |
| **S.R. Bommai** (1994) | **Federalism**, **secularism** and democracy are basic |
| **L. Chandra Kumar** (1997) | **7 judges**; judicial review by High Courts (**Art 226/227**) and the SC (**Art 32**) is basic; tribunals are under HC review |
| **M. Nagaraj** (2006) | Upheld the **77th, 81st, 82nd and 85th** Amendments, with conditions |
| **I.R. Coelho** (2007) | **9 judges**; Ninth Schedule laws added after **24 April 1973** are tested against the basic structure |
| **NJAC case** (16 October 2015) | **Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union**; **4:1** struck down the **99th Amendment** and the NJAC Act — **independence of the judiciary**; **J. Chelameswar** dissented; the **collegium** revived |
| **Janhit Abhiyan** (7 November 2022) | **5 judges**, **3:2** upheld the **103rd (EWS)** Amendment |

### Elements of the basic structure (as recognised so far)
- **Supremacy of the Constitution**; sovereign, democratic and republican form; **secularism**; **separation of powers**; **federalism**; unity and integrity; welfare state.
- **Judicial review**; **independence of the judiciary**; **rule of law**; **free and fair elections**; parliamentary system.
- **Limited amending power**; harmony between Fundamental Rights and DPSPs; principle of equality; freedom and dignity of the individual; effective access to justice; powers of the SC under **Art 32, 136, 141 and 142**.
- The list is **not in the Constitution** — it is judge-made and open (UPSC 2020).

## Don't confuse
- **Golaknath** — 11 judges, 6:5; **Kesavananda** — 13 judges, 7:6.
- **Raj Narain** (1975) first struck a constitutional provision; **Minerva Mills** (1980) struck the 42nd's Art 368(4), (5).
- NJAC was struck down in **2015**; the EWS amendment was **upheld** in **2022**.

**TL;DR**
- Shankari Prasad 1951 → Sajjan Singh 1965 → Golaknath 1967 → 24th Amendment 1971 → Kesavananda 1973.
- Raj Narain 1975, Minerva 1980, Waman Rao 1981, Sambamurthy 1987 (AP), Kihoto 1992, Chandra Kumar 1997, Coelho 2007, NJAC 2015, Janhit Abhiyan 2022.
keyPoints: Golaknath (1967) was decided by 11 judges, 6:5, under CJ K. Subba Rao, applying prospective overruling.
Kesavananda Bharati (24 April 1973) was decided by 13 judges, 7:6, under CJ S.M. Sikri; the petitioner headed the Edneer Mutt in Kerala.
Minerva Mills (1980) held that limited amending power and harmony between Fundamental Rights and DPSPs are basic features.
P. Sambamurthy v. State of AP (1987) struck down the Art 371D clause letting the State Government override the Administrative Tribunal.
L. Chandra Kumar (1997) made judicial review under Art 226/227 and Art 32 part of the basic structure.
The NJAC case (16 October 2015) struck down the 99th Amendment 4:1; Janhit Abhiyan (2022) upheld the 103rd EWS Amendment 3:2.

items.title: For Mains — Amendments & the Basic Structure
items.body:
## For Mains — how to use this topic in answers

This topic feeds **Paper III (mains-3)**, under the Judiciary / judicial review / amendments clause (syllabus M3-5) and the Constitution clause (M3-1). Mains answers must move beyond 'which amendment did what' to argue how the amending power and the basic-structure doctrine balance **parliamentary sovereignty** against **constitutional supremacy**.

**Dimensions Mains asks**

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Need / rationale | A living Constitution must adapt; a rigid-only document would break under social change |
| Features | Three-tier procedure (Article 368) blends rigidity and flexibility; graded majorities protect federalism |
| Significance | Basic-structure doctrine preserves constitutional identity against transient majorities |
| Criticism / limits | 'Basic structure' is undefined and open-ended, giving judges wide, unaccountable discretion |
| Way forward | Judicial self-restraint, reasoned use of the doctrine, and respect for the elected legislature's domain |

**Facts, cases and reports to quote**
- **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** — 13-judge bench; the doctrine's origin.
- **Minerva Mills (1980)** — judicial review and limited amending power are basic features.
- **I.R. Coelho (2007)** — Ninth Schedule laws post-24 April 1973 are reviewable.
- **NJAC case (99th Amendment, 2015)** — struck down to protect judicial independence, showing the doctrine still bites.
- Over **106 amendments** since 1951 show the document's working flexibility.
- The doctrine has influenced courts in Bangladesh, Pakistan and other Commonwealth states.

**The AP angle**
The AP Reorganisation Act, 2014 and later boundary and local-body changes show how ordinary and special majorities are used in practice; a candidate can cite state reorganisation as an example of flexibility within the federal scheme.

**Use in answers**
- Open with the rigidity-versus-flexibility framing, then anchor each claim to a named case.
- Quote: 'The Constitution is not an end but a means to an end' (reflecting the Kesavananda balance).
- Diagram idea: a simple balance-scale with 'Parliament's amending power' on one pan and 'basic structure' on the other.
keyPoints: Feeds mains-3 (Judiciary / judicial review / amendments, M3-5; Constitution, M3-1).
Frame answers as parliamentary sovereignty vs constitutional supremacy.
Quote Kesavananda (1973), Minerva Mills (1980), I.R. Coelho (2007), NJAC (2015).
Criticism: 'basic structure' is undefined, giving judges wide discretion.
Way forward: judicial restraint and respect for the elected legislature's domain.
